questions.knowledge_point: Obtaining a Higher-Order Derivative Of a Function Given its Higher-Degree Taylor Polynomial
questions.problem:
The fifth-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=2$ is given by

$$
{P}_{5}(x)=(x-2)-\frac{1}{2}(x-2)^{2}+\frac{1}{3}(x-2)^{3}-\frac{1}{4}(x-2)^{4}+\frac{1}{5}(x-2)^{5}.
$$

What is ${f}^{(4)}(2)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The coefficient of $(x-2)^{4}$ is given by $\frac{{f}^{(4)}(2)}{4!}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{f}^{(4)}(2)}{4!} & =-\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{{f}^{(4)}(2)}{24} & =-\frac{1}{4} \\ {f}^{(4)}(2) & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The fourth-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=0$ is given by

$$
{P}_{4}(x)=1+\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{8}{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{16}{x}^{3}-\frac{3}{64}{x}^{4}.
$$

What is ${f}^{‴}(0)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The coefficient of ${x}^{3}$ is given by $\frac{{f}^{‴}(0)}{3!}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{f}^{‴}(0)}{3!} & =\frac{1}{16} \\ \frac{{f}^{‴}(0)}{6} & =\frac{1}{16} \\ {f}^{‴}(0) & =\frac{3}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

{{field-1}}

questions.knowledge_point: Computing a Higher-Degree Taylor Polynomial Of a Given Function About a Given Point
questions.worked_solution:
The fourth-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{4}(x)= & \,f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+\frac{{f}^{‴}(a)}{3!}(x-a)^{3} \\  & \,+\frac{{f}^{(4)}(a)}{4!}(x-a)^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have $a=\frac{\pi }{3},$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{4}(x)= & \,f(\frac{\pi }{3})+{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3})(x-\frac{\pi }{3})+\frac{{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{3})}{2!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{3})}^{2} \\  & \,+\frac{{f}^{‴}(\frac{\pi }{3})}{3!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{3})}^{3}+\frac{{f}^{(4)}(\frac{\pi }{3})}{4!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{3})}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So we need to work out $f(\frac{\pi }{3}),$ ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3}),$ ${f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{3}),$ ${f}^{‴}(\frac{\pi }{3})$ and ${f}^{(4)}(\frac{\pi }{3}),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) & ⟹ &  & f\,(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )=-1 \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{′}\,(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )=0 \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-9\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{″}\,(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =-9\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )=9 \\ {f}^{‴}(x) & =27\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{‴}\,(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =27\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )=0 \\ {f}^{(4)}(x) & =81\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) & ⟹ &  & {f}^{(4)}\,(\frac{\pi }{3}) & =81\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )=-81\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${P}_{4}(x)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{4}(x) & =-1+0(x-\frac{\pi }{3})+\frac{9}{2!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{3})}^{2}+0{(x-\frac{\pi }{3})}^{3}-\frac{81}{4!}{(x-\frac{\pi }{3})}^{4} \\  & =-1+\frac{9}{2}{(x-\frac{\pi }{3})}^{2}-\frac{27}{8}{(x-\frac{\pi }{3})}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
